headline: Amazon's careers copy centers on customer obsession, high-bar performance, and scale-driven invention — with DEI language that peaked in 2017–18 and has since narrowed.
identity: Amazon has consistently valued customer obsession, high-performance standards, and invention at scale, with phrases like 'Earth's most customer-centric company,' 'relentlessly high standards,' and 'a place where builders can build' appearing across nearly every year of data. Diversity and inclusion language surged sharply in 2017–18 — when the copy featured dedicated sections on affinity groups, pay equity, and explicit demographic categories including race, disability, and LGBTQ identity — but contracted significantly after 2019, reverting to brief aspirational mentions ('We strive to reflect the diversity of our customers') and dropping specific demographic terms like 'Black,' 'LGBTQ,' and 'disability' entirely from the copy by 2019. Altruism and community-benefit framing, which spiked in 2017 around programs like 'Black to the Future' and Code.org partnerships, has also receded, replaced by a more transactional upskilling pitch ('investing billions of dollars to help our employees and our neighbors prepare for the jobs of the future') in 2025–26.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are driven by customer outcomes above all else, comfortable with explicitly high and self-described 'unreasonably high' standards, and energized by large-scale invention — the copy consistently reaches for people who 'think big,' treat frugality as a virtue, and see themselves as 'pioneers' building something that has 'only just begun.'

sections.heading: The Unchanging Core: Customer Obsession and High Standards
sections.body:
From 2007 through 2026, the careers copy returns to the same anchors: 'Our mission is to be Earth's most customer-centric company' and the Leadership Principles framing of relentlessly high bars. The 2007 page asked hiring managers 'Will I admire this person? Is this person a superstar?' The 2016 expansion of the site added explicit LP headers — 'Insist on the Highest Standards,' 'Hire and Develop the Best,' 'Bias for Action' — and those have remained stable ever since.

Performance-axis scores confirm this: zscores for performance language were above average in 2007, 2011, 2016, and 2026, with no year showing a sustained retreat. The meritocracy signal tracks similarly, staying consistently above peer average in years with rich copy. This is the most durable thread in the data.

sections.heading: The DEI Arc: Peak in 2017–18, Quiet Retreat After 2019
sections.body:
The inclusion signal is the most volatile in the dataset. Before 2016, DEI language was effectively absent — the register classification shows 'absent' for all chunks in 2007–2013. In 2016 a dedicated 'Diversity at Amazon' section appeared, listing demographic sources ('gender, race, age, national origin, sexual orientation, culture, education'). By 2017 the copy had expanded to 131 chunks, with 25 classified as 'aspirational_vague' and 2 as 'structural_process,' and featured named affinity groups (Black Employee Network, Latinos@Amazon, Glamazon), pay equity commitments, and community outreach narratives. Inclusion zscores hit their peak: +1.54 in 2017.

After 2018 the page shrank dramatically. By 2019 the copy was down to 4 chunks with only one aspirational_vague register hit. Terms like 'Black,' 'LGBTQ,' 'disability,' and 'accessibility' disappeared from the lexicon after 2018. The phrase 'Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion' persisted as a one-line section header through 2024 ('We strive to reflect the diversity of our customers, vendors, and communities') but without the substantive copy that surrounded it in 2017–18. In 2025–26 the framing shifted toward workforce representation data ('We track the representation of women and underrepresented communities because we know that diversity helps us build better teams') — a more business-case register than the belonging-and-community language of 2017.

sections.heading: Recent Shift: Scale, Upskilling, and Wellbeing Replace Community Narrative
sections.body:
From 2023 onward the careers copy leans on a different set of signals. Wellbeing language — benefits, wages, safety — rose to above-average zscores in 2023 (+1.05), 2025 (+1.32), and 2026 (+1.37), with specific wage figures cited ('average starting pay of $19 per hour,' 'average total compensation package... over $29 per hour') and safety statistics ('reduced workplace injury rates by 43% since 2019'). This is a notable shift from the 2007–2018 era, when wellbeing language was near zero or negative.

Altruism scores, which peaked in 2017–18 around community hackathons and STEM pipeline programs, have returned to near-2016 levels by 2023–24, though 2025–26 show a modest uptick tied to upskilling framing ('investing billions of dollars to help our employees and our neighbors'). Techno-optimism, strong in 2007–2013 with explicit references to AWS, Kindle, and computer science culture, has flattened to near-zero since 2019 — the copy no longer leads with technology excitement. The overall picture in 2025–26 is a company describing itself as a large, stable employer with competitive pay and benefits, united by customer obsession, with diversity framed as a business input rather than a cultural commitment.
